passage: Sand flew as Ganga swung the plastic spade, and it cracked against Usha's knuckles. Usha howled. The preschool teacher knelt between them in the sandpit. “Ganga, what do you say?” “Sorry,” Ganga muttered to the sand, already reaching for her bucket. The teacher gently turned her shoulders. “Look at Usha's hand. It's red, see? What could help it?” Ganga stared at the knuckle, then ran to the tap and came back with a dripping cloth. She pressed it on very carefully. “Sorry I hit it,” she said again, quieter, and handed Usha the spade first.

qa.q: What did Ganga bring back from the tap?
qa.a: Ganga came back with a dripping cloth and pressed it on Usha's hand.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when she first muttered sorry to the sand?
qa.a: She was most likely embarrassed and keen to get back to playing, since she looked away and reached for her bucket; she may also have felt a little scared of being in trouble.

qa.q: How did the teacher help the sorry become real?
qa.a: The teacher asked Ganga to look at the red knuckle and think of what could help, so Ganga saw the hurt and did something to repair it.

qa.q: How might Usha feel about the second sorry compared with the first?
qa.a: Usha probably felt more comforted by the second one, because it came with a cool cloth and the spade handed to her first.

grounding: Shows a prompted sorry turning into a real apology once the child looks at the hurt and helps to repair it.

passage: My little brother Joseph threw his ball too hard yesterday, and it hit the girl from flat 4B on the nose. I'm Nandini; I was on the park bench with my homework. Her mother said, “Say sorry, Joseph.” He said “sorry” so fast it sounded like one sneeze, then ran after the ball. The girl kept crying. Joseph came back slowly. He stood watching her rub her nose, his own face crumpling. Then he held out the ball. “You keep it first. Does it still hurt?” I don't know what he was thinking, but she laughed through her tears.

qa.q: Where was Nandini sitting when the ball hit the girl?
qa.a: Nandini was on the park bench with her homework.

qa.q: What does Joseph's crumpling face suggest about how he felt when he came back?
qa.a: It suggests he felt sorry and worried once he saw her rubbing her nose; he might also have been upset that the game had stopped.

qa.q: What could the girl's mother do next time to help Joseph's sorry mean more?
qa.a: She could pause after the quick sorry and ask Joseph to look at how the girl was feeling, then let him choose a way to help.

qa.q: How does Nandini see the difference between Joseph's two sorries?
qa.a: Nandini notices the first sorry was rushed like a sneeze, while the second came with the ball and a question, and that one made the girl laugh.

grounding: Shows a quick prompted sorry followed by a truer apology when the child notices the hurt and offers something to make it better.

passage: Monday: Vaibhav raced his tricycle round the courtyard and ran over Sarita's toe. Mummy made him say sorry. He shouted it and pedalled off. Sarita limped home. Wednesday: Sarita would not come out to play. Vaibhav sat on the step, watching her gate. “Is her toe still broken?” he asked Mummy. “Not broken, just sore. And she's sad.” He went quiet for a long time. Saturday: Vaibhav knocked on Sarita's door holding his tricycle bell. “Sorry I bumped your toe. You can ring it.” Then he pushed the tricycle slowly beside her, all the way round the courtyard.

qa.q: On which day did Vaibhav knock on Sarita's door?
qa.a: Vaibhav knocked on Sarita's door on Saturday.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav have been feeling as he sat on the step on Wednesday?
qa.a: He was probably lonely and a bit guilty, since he kept watching her gate and asked about her toe; he may simply have missed his playmate too.

qa.q: How did Mummy's answer on Wednesday help Vaibhav change?
qa.a: She told him plainly that the toe was sore and Sarita was sad, which linked his bump to her feelings and gave him time to think of a better sorry.

qa.q: What was Monday's sorry like for Sarita compared with Saturday's?
qa.a: On Monday the shouted sorry did nothing for her sore toe, but on Saturday she got a real sorry, the bell to ring and a slow walk beside him.

grounding: Shows a prompted sorry on the first day growing into a real apology days later, once the child sees the friend's hurt and helps make up for it.

passage: Class note, Tuesday. Written by Sangeeta, KG teacher. Today I held up Preeti's leaf print and told the whole class it was the neatest one. Preeti clapped both hands over her face and giggled, peeking through her fingers, then slid behind her friend. Later she spilled the green paint and did the same thing: face hidden, giggle high and shaky. I think both moments were about being looked at. I didn't mention the spill aloud. I knelt beside her, handed her a cloth and whispered, “Spills happen.” Tomorrow I'll tell her about good work quietly at her table.

qa.q: What did Preeti do when her leaf print was held up?
qa.a: Preeti clapped both hands over her face and giggled, peeking through her fingers.

qa.q: Why might Preeti have hidden her face both times?
qa.a: She most likely felt embarrassed at everyone looking at her, whether for praise or for the spill; the first giggle could also carry a little pleasure mixed with shyness.

qa.q: What change does Sangeeta plan, and why might it help?
qa.a: She plans to praise Preeti quietly at her table, which lets Preeti enjoy the praise without the whole class watching.

qa.q: What would change if Sangeeta had pointed out the spill to the class?
qa.a: Preeti would likely have felt more exposed and ashamed, and she might hide or avoid painting next time.

grounding: Shows a preschooler hiding the face and giggling when noticed for both praise and a mistake, and a teacher choosing kind, private handling.

passage: The milk can clanged on the road outside Thomas's tea shop, and Madhav landed on his knees beside it. The men on the bench turned to look. Madhav sprang up, both palms over his eyes, giggling in thin little bursts. One man started to laugh too. Thomas raised a hand to stop him, then stepped out and crouched. “The can's fine. Knees fine?” he asked, low. Madhav nodded behind his fingers. Thomas walked him round the side of the shop, away from the bench, and filled the can again. “I tripped on that same stone last week,” he said.

qa.q: What did Madhav drop outside the tea shop?
qa.a: Madhav dropped the milk can, and it clanged on the road.

qa.q: What were Madhav's giggles and covered eyes most likely showing?
qa.a: They most likely showed embarrassment at the men watching his fall; he could also have been shaken or a little hurt and hiding it.

qa.q: Which of Thomas's choices protected Madhav's feelings?
qa.a: Thomas stopped the laughing, spoke low, moved Madhav away from the bench and shared his own trip on the same stone.

qa.q: How might the man who began to laugh see the moment after Thomas raised his hand?
qa.a: He might realise his laugh would have added to the boy's embarrassment, and that the giggling was nerves, not fun.

grounding: Shows a young child covering the eyes and giggling nervously when others notice a mistake, and an adult handling it kindly and privately.

passage: In the bakery queue, Ulla told the woman behind them, “Sami zipped his own snowsuit today, all by himself!” Sami pushed his face into his grandmother's coat and giggled, a squeaky sound, and would not come out. The woman smiled. “Clever boy!” Sami giggled harder and pulled the coat right over his head. Ulla stopped talking about it. Walking home through the snow, she said, just to him, “I was proud of that zip.” Sami held her hand and said, “Don't tell the shop people. Tell only me.”

qa.q: What had Sami done by himself that day?
qa.a: Sami zipped his own snowsuit by himself.

qa.q: How can you tell that Sami felt embarrassed rather than simply happy?
qa.a: He hid in Ulla's coat, giggled squeakily and later asked her to tell only him, which points to embarrassment at strangers hearing, though he was probably pleased with the praise too 🙂

qa.q: Which of Ulla's choices helped Sami, and why?
qa.a: She stopped talking to the stranger and praised him quietly on the walk home, so he could enjoy the praise without an audience.

qa.q: If you were Ulla, what would you want to remember next time?
qa.a: That Sami enjoys praise best in private, so a quiet word may mean more to him than telling others.

grounding: Shows a young child hiding the face and giggling when praised in front of strangers, and how private praise suits the child better.

passage: The children call me Sudha Aunty. I was hanging washing when the boy downstairs started crying; his kite had torn on the gate. Parul, from the next flat, stopped skipping. She watched him a moment, then trotted over and hugged him hard around the middle, rope still in her hand. He kept crying. She pulled back, frowned, and held out her skipping rope instead. I can't know what went on in that small head. But when her mother came down, she said, “Parul, you saw he was sad and wanted him to feel better. That's caring.” Parul nodded seriously.

qa.q: What had happened to the boy's kite?
qa.a: His kite had torn on the gate.

qa.q: Why did Parul hold out her skipping rope after the hug?
qa.a: She seems to have felt concerned and wanted him to stop being sad, so when the hug didn't work she tried a gift; she may also have felt unsure what else to do.

qa.q: How did Parul's mother help her learn from this moment?
qa.a: She named what Parul had noticed and done, linking the boy's sadness to Parul's caring, which helps Parul understand her own kindness.

qa.q: How does Sudha see what Parul was thinking?
qa.a: Sudha only sees the actions and admits she cannot know Parul's thoughts, but the hug and the rope look to her like simple, real care.

grounding: Shows a young child offering a hug and then a toy to a crying child, and an adult naming the feeling behind it.

passage: Monday: Mahima cried at the preschool gate when her papa left. Baljeet stood by the shoe rack, staring, thumb in mouth. Tuesday: Mahima cried again. Baljeet walked over, pushed his toy tractor into her hands and said, “Vroom.” She sniffed and held it. The teacher crouched beside them. “Baljeet, you saw Mahima was sad, so you shared. That's kind.” Baljeet grinned. Thursday: A new boy wailed by the door. Baljeet looked at Mahima. Together they carried the tractor over, and Baljeet patted the boy's arm. “Sad. Here.”

qa.q: What toy did Baljeet give Mahima?
qa.a: Baljeet pushed his toy tractor into her hands.

qa.q: What might Baljeet have been feeling as he stared on Monday?
qa.a: He was probably puzzled and a little worried by her crying, though he might just have been shy or curious in the new place.

qa.q: How did the teacher's words on Tuesday help Baljeet?
qa.a: By saying that he saw Mahima was sad and shared, the teacher linked her feeling to his kind act, so he could use it again on Thursday.

qa.q: What was the tractor like for Mahima on Tuesday?
qa.a: It gave her something to hold and showed that someone had noticed her, so she sniffed and calmed a little instead of crying alone.

grounding: Shows a young child's simple sympathy, a shared toy and a pat, growing after an adult names the link between feelings and care.

passage: The band was so loud at the wedding that nobody heard Jyoti cry. She had pinched her finger in a folding chair and sat under the table, sobbing. Hemant, crawling after a balloon, found her. He looked at her finger, then at her face. He wrapped both arms round her, awkward and tight, then pushed his half-eaten laddoo into her good hand. When that didn't help, he ran out and tugged his Masi's sari until she bent down. Masi scooped Jyoti up and said to him, “You saw she was hurting and you brought help. That was caring, Hemant.”

qa.q: Where did Hemant find Jyoti?
qa.a: Hemant found her under the table, sobbing.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when he looked at her finger and then her face?
qa.a: He likely felt worried and sorry for her, which shows in his tight hug and the laddoo; he may also have felt a bit helpless when neither worked.

qa.q: Which of Hemant's choices helped most, and why?
qa.a: Fetching his Masi helped most, because in the loud hall an adult could look after the pinched finger when a hug and a sweet could not.

qa.q: What would change if the band had been quiet?
qa.a: An adult might have heard Jyoti straight away, and Hemant would not have had to find her and bring help himself.

grounding: Shows a young child offering a hug and a sweet to a crying child in a noisy place, and an adult naming the act as caring.

passage: The school van honked twice, and Reena was still tying her son Chaitanya's shoelace on the steps. He wasn't helping. He had tilted his head at the ground, frowning. “Huh? My shadow was behind me. Now it's in front.” Reena glanced at her watch. “Quick idea,” she said, turning him round. “Where's the sun?” He squinted over his shoulder. “There.” “Now walk to the van and watch the shadow.” Chaitanya marched, looking down, then turned and walked back three steps. “It goes away from the sun!” he shouted, climbing in. Reena laughed and waved.

qa.q: What was puzzling Chaitanya about his shadow?
qa.a: His shadow was behind him before, and now it was in front.

qa.q: What do Chaitanya's tilted head and frown suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest he felt puzzled and curious because something didn't fit; he might also have been stalling because he didn't want to rush.

qa.q: How did Reena handle the puzzle even though the van was waiting?
qa.a: She asked one quick question about the sun and let him test it on his way to the van, so he found the answer himself without making them late.

qa.q: How might the van driver see the delay?
qa.a: The driver might feel impatient during the wait, not knowing a small science idea was being tried out on the steps.

grounding: Shows a preschooler tilting the head, frowning and saying huh at something that doesn't fit, and a parent explaining simply and letting him test the idea.

passage: On a hot afternoon in their Chandigarh flat, Gurleen stared at her glass of nimbu pani. Tiny drops were running down the outside. She tilted her head and frowned. “Huh? It's leaking. But there's no hole.” Her aunt Ankita put down her phone. “What's inside the glass?” “Ice.” “Touch the outside.” “Cold!” Ankita took a steel spoon from the fridge and breathed on it; it fogged. “The air has water in it. It sticks to cold things.” Gurleen grabbed the spoon and breathed on it herself, then on the glass, then on the window, checking which ones went cloudy.

qa.q: What did Gurleen see on the outside of her glass?
qa.a: Tiny drops were running down the outside of the glass.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen say the glass was leaking?
qa.a: She felt puzzled because the drops didn't fit what she knew, since there was no hole; she might also have been a little worried her drink was spilling.

qa.q: What could Ankita try if Gurleen still didn't understand?
qa.a: She could let Gurleen put ice in another glass and watch drops form on it, so she tests the idea again with her own hands.

qa.q: What would change if Ankita had said it was nothing and gone back to her phone?
qa.a: Gurleen would lose a chance to try ideas and might stop asking, and her puzzle would stay unanswered.

grounding: Shows a preschooler tilting the head, frowning and saying huh when drops appear on a glass, and an adult explaining simply and letting her try.

passage: “Ammi, why is the moon coming with us?” “Hmm. Is it?” Noor pressed her nose to the car window, head tilted. “Huh? We turned. It's still there. It's following.” “What do you think?” asked Sabina, her Ammi, from the driver's seat. “Maybe it likes our car.” “Maybe. Let's test. See that lamp post? Watch it.” “It went behind!” “And the moon?” “Still there.” Noor frowned. “The lamp post is near. The moon is… far far?” “Very far. Far things look like they stay put.” “So it's not following.” A pause. “Can it still like our car?” Sabina laughed. “It can.”

qa.q: What did Sabina ask Noor to watch?
qa.a: Sabina asked Noor to watch the lamp post.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when the moon was still there after the turn?
qa.a: She felt puzzled and a bit excited, since it didn't fit and she guessed the moon liked their car; her tilted head suggests real wondering 🤔

qa.q: Why did the lamp post test work well?
qa.a: It let Noor compare something near with something far and reach the idea herself instead of just being told.

qa.q: If you were Sabina, driving at night, what would you want Noor to take from this?
qa.a: That puzzles can be tested and that her guesses are welcome, even the playful one about the moon liking the car.

grounding: Shows a young child frowning, tilting the head and saying huh when the moon seems to follow, and a parent explaining simply while letting her try ideas.

passage: I'm Pradeep, and my little brother Arnab asked Dadi eleven questions before lunch. I counted. “Why do I have a belly button?” “Why is yours bigger?” “Why can't I see my own ears?” Dadi was shelling peas. She didn't shoo him away. “The belly button is where you were joined to your Ma before you were born.” Arnab lifted his shirt and poked it, frowning. “Why?” “So you could get food inside her.” He went quiet, then asked, “Did I eat peas?” Dadi laughed and handed him a pod to open. He stayed by her all morning.

qa.q: What was Dadi doing while Arnab asked questions?
qa.a: Dadi was shelling peas.

qa.q: What does Arnab's poking and frowning suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt curious and a bit puzzled, trying to fit the answer to his own body; he might also have found the idea funny.

qa.q: How did Dadi keep Arnab's questions welcome?
qa.a: She gave short, honest answers without shooing him away and handed him a pea pod, so he felt his asking was welcome.

qa.q: How does Pradeep see the eleven questions?
qa.a: Pradeep counts them almost like a joke, yet notices that Arnab stayed near Dadi all morning, as if the answers made him feel close to her.

grounding: Shows a young child asking why again and again about the body, and an adult giving honest, simple answers that build trust.

passage: Sunday: “Why does rain fall? Why from clouds? Why are clouds up?” Mridul followed his papa, Ramesh, round the kitchen. Ramesh stopped stirring. “I know a bit, not all. Let's find out together.” Tuesday: They boiled water in a pot and held a cold steel plate over it. Drops gathered underneath and fell. “Rain!” Mridul shouted. “Why does it fall?” “Too heavy to stay up,” said Ramesh. Friday: Thunder rolled over the school yard. Mridul told his friend, “Clouds are water. When drops get heavy they fall. Me and my papa made it.” Then he frowned. “But why is thunder?”

qa.q: What did Mridul and Ramesh hold over the boiling pot?
qa.a: They held a cold steel plate over the pot.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel when the drops fell from the plate?
qa.a: He felt excited and proud, shouting “Rain!”, though his next why shows he was still curious rather than finished.

qa.q: Why was Ramesh's answer on Sunday a good choice?
qa.a: He admitted he did not know everything and offered a shared search, which kept Mridul's trust and turned the questions into something they did together.

qa.q: What is it like for Ramesh when Mridul follows him with question after question?
qa.a: It may feel tiring in the middle of cooking, but Ramesh chose to stop stirring, which shows he valued the questions.

grounding: Shows a young child asking why about rain over several days, and a parent's honest answer and shared experiment building trust.

passage: Horns blared at the crossing, and rain drummed on Rekha's umbrella. Vidya tugged her hand. “Why do we wait? The road is empty there.” “The light is red for us,” Rekha said, bending close so Vidya could hear. “Why?” “So cars know it's their turn.” “Why do they get a turn?” A bus roared past, spraying water. Rekha didn't say because I said so. She pointed. “See how big that bus is? It can't stop fast. The light keeps us safe from it.” When the little green man lit up, she said, “Now it's our turn,” and marched.

qa.q: What did Rekha point to when she explained the light?
qa.a: Rekha pointed to the big bus.

qa.q: Why might Vidya keep asking why at the crossing?
qa.a: She was probably curious and a bit impatient, because the road looked empty to her; the questions show she was trying to understand the rule, not just being difficult.

qa.q: What small step helped Rekha answer in the noise?
qa.a: She bent close and used the passing bus as a quick, honest example instead of saying because I said so.

qa.q: How would the walk feel for Vidya if Rekha had snapped at her questions?
qa.a: Vidya might feel her questions were a nuisance and stop trusting that rules have reasons.

grounding: Shows a young child asking why again and again about a road rule, and an adult giving honest, simple answers despite the noise and rain.

passage: I'm Seema, and on Saturdays I help at the library's storytime. When the reader asked who wanted to turn the pages, Nandini shot up off the mat, arm stretched so high she was on tiptoe. “Me first! Me! Me first!” Two smaller children shrank back. The reader smiled and held up a little wooden spoon. “Whoever holds the spoon turns the page. It goes round the circle.” Nandini sat, bouncing, eyes on the spoon as it travelled. Her knees jiggled the whole time. When it reached her, she turned the page very carefully, then passed the spoon on.

qa.q: What did the reader hold up?
qa.a: The reader held up a little wooden spoon.

qa.q: What do Nandini's jiggling knees suggest while she waited?
qa.a: They suggest she was still excited and impatient, keen for her turn; she may also have felt proud when she finally got it.

qa.q: Why did the spoon rule work better than telling Nandini to calm down?
qa.a: It gave her a clear way to see when her turn would come, so her eagerness had somewhere to go while she waited.

qa.q: What was storytime like for the two smaller children before the spoon appeared?
qa.a: They shrank back, so they may have felt crowded out and unsure they'd ever get a turn.

grounding: Shows a preschooler jumping up and shouting me first, and a simple turn-taking rule helping her manage the wait.

passage: Monday: “Me first! Me first!” Karthik leapt up so fast his chair tipped over when Miss Elizabeth lifted the watering can. He reached the tulsi pot first. Wednesday: Miss Elizabeth taped a paper chain of names beside the door and clipped a peg on the first one. “Each day, the next name waters.” Karthik's name was third. He groaned, jumped and touched it every morning. Friday: The peg reached Karthik. He hopped to the door, then carried the can slowly with both hands. Afterwards he moved the peg on himself and told the girl beside him, “Monday it's yours.”

qa.q: Where was Karthik's name on the paper chain?
qa.a: Karthik's name was third on the paper chain.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when he groaned and touched his name each morning?
qa.a: He felt impatient and eager, but touching the name suggests he was also looking forward to it and trusting his turn would come.

qa.q: What made the paper chain helpful for a child like Karthik?
qa.a: It showed him exactly when his turn would be, so waiting became something he could see and count.

qa.q: How might the girl beside Karthik feel when he tells her Monday is hers?
qa.a: She would probably feel pleased and included, since the eager boy who used to rush now hands the turn on.

grounding: Shows a preschooler leaping up and shouting me first, and a visible turn-taking rule helping him manage the wait over several days.

passage: Rain kept everyone indoors, and there were only five minutes before the vans came. “One riddle each,” said Keerthana Miss. “What has four legs and says moo?” Pallavi was already on her feet, hand waving. “Me first! I know! Me!” Keerthana crouched to her level. “Hands up, lips shut, bottom on the mat. I pick someone new each time.” Pallavi sat down hard, lips pressed together, hand trembling in the air. Three riddles went to others. Her face crumpled. For the last riddle, “What is round and shines at night?”, Keerthana pointed to her. “The moon!” Pallavi yelled, beaming.

qa.q: How many riddles went to others before Pallavi's turn?
qa.a: Three riddles went to others.

qa.q: What does Pallavi's crumpled face suggest after the third riddle?
qa.a: It suggests she felt disappointed and worried she would miss out; she may also have been finding the waiting very hard.

qa.q: How did Keerthana's rule suit the short time?
qa.a: The simple rule of hands up, lips shut and someone new each time kept the game fair and quick, and she still made sure the eager child got a turn.

qa.q: What would change if Keerthana had let the loudest child answer every time?
qa.a: Pallavi might answer every riddle while quieter children got none, and she would not learn that waiting still brings a turn.

grounding: Shows a preschooler jumping up and shouting me first, and a clear turn-taking rule helping her manage the wait under time pressure.

passage: “Mumma, I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow. I hope, I hope, I hope.” Gopika held up both hands, fingers crossed so hard they went white. “The sky looks grey,” said Alka, her mother, folding the picnic mat. “It might rain.” “If I keep them crossed, it won't.” “Crossing fingers is a way of wishing. The clouds don't know about it.” Gopika frowned. “Then what's the use?” “It shows you want it. If it rains, what could we do?” “…Picnic on the floor?” “On the balcony, with the mat.” Gopika uncrossed one hand. “Okay. But I'm still hoping.” “Me too.”

qa.q: What was Alka folding?
qa.a: Alka was folding the picnic mat.

qa.q: Why did Gopika cross her fingers so hard?
qa.a: She felt hopeful and a bit anxious about the grey sky, believing her wish might keep the rain away.

qa.q: How did Alka prepare Gopika for a possible letdown?
qa.a: She said honestly it might rain and asked Gopika what they could do if it did, so a balcony picnic became the backup.

qa.q: If you were Alka, why would you still say “Me too”?
qa.a: To show Gopika that hoping is fine and shared, even while planning for rain 🙂

grounding: Shows a young child crossing fingers and repeating a hope about picnic weather, and a parent's honest, gentle talk preparing for a letdown.

passage: Observation note, Thursday. Divyansh, nursery teacher. Mridul has checked his bean cup six times today. Each time he crouches, crosses the fingers on both hands and whispers, “Please come up, please come up before Friday.” Friday is when the children take their cups home. Three cups have sprouted; his has not. After snack I sat with him and said some seeds are slow and his might not show by Friday. His lip wobbled. We made a plan: if it hasn't sprouted, he takes it home with a card saying “Still sleeping” and tells me about it on Monday.

qa.q: How many cups had sprouted?
qa.a: Three cups had sprouted, but Mridul's had not.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling as he whispered to his bean cup?
qa.a: He felt hopeful and anxious, wishing hard for the seed to come up before Friday; his wobbling lip later shows disappointment starting.

qa.q: What did Divyansh do that prepared Mridul for a letdown?
qa.a: Divyansh told Mridul honestly the seed might not show by Friday and made a plan with the “Still sleeping” card, so the hope had a gentle landing.

qa.q: What would change if Divyansh had promised the bean would come up?
qa.a: Mridul might feel tricked and more upset on Friday, and trust Divyansh less next time.

grounding: Shows a young child crossing fingers and repeating a hopeful wish, and a teacher's honest, gentle talk preparing for a possible letdown.

passage: The village bus rattled towards the Baisakhi mela, and Baljeet sat on Lalit Chacha's knee, chanting at the window. “I hope the big wheel is going. I hope the big wheel is going.” His fingers were crossed on both hands. Lalit looked at the dust blowing across the fields. “Baljeet, it's very windy. Sometimes they stop the big wheel in wind.” The chanting stopped. “Forever?” “Just till the wind drops. If it's stopped, we'll see the bangle stalls first and come back.” When they arrived, the wheel stood still. Baljeet's lip shook. Then he tugged Lalit's kurta. “Bangles first, then.”

qa.q: What did Baljeet chant at the bus window?
qa.a: Baljeet chanted, “I hope the big wheel is going.”

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when the wheel stood still?
qa.a: He felt disappointed, shown by his shaking lip, but also a little ready, since he remembered the bangle plan.

qa.q: Why did Lalit mention the wind before they arrived?
qa.a: So Baljeet's hope came with an honest warning and a backup plan, making the letdown easier to handle.

qa.q: What might it be like for Lalit to watch Baljeet's lip shake?
qa.a: Lalit might feel sad for him but relieved that the earlier talk helped him cope.

grounding: Shows a young child crossing fingers and repeating a hope, and an adult's honest, gentle words preparing him for a letdown.

passage: In the clinic waiting room, Aditi wrestled with her cardigan for ages, tongue poking out. Then she jumped off the plastic chair. “Look! Look, Amma!” Every button was done, one hole skipped near the bottom. Vasudha put down the appointment card and looked, properly. “You did those yourself. You kept trying even when the top one slipped.” Aditi grinned and puffed out her chest. The man across the aisle said, “What a genius!” Aditi glanced at him, then back at her mother, and pointed at the skipped hole. “That one's wrong. I'll fix it.” And she did.

qa.q: Where was Aditi when she buttoned her cardigan?
qa.a: Aditi was in the clinic waiting room.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel after finishing the buttons?
qa.a: She felt proud, grinning and puffing out her chest; the big praise from the stranger seemed to matter less to her than her mother really looking.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha's words fit better than “What a genius”?
qa.a: Vasudha named the real effort of trying again, which Aditi could use, while “genius” was big praise that did not describe what she had done.

qa.q: How might the man across the aisle see his compliment?
qa.a: He probably meant it kindly and may not notice that Aditi looked back to her mother, whose attention mattered more.

grounding: Shows a preschooler holding up a finished task and saying look, and a parent's attention to real effort mattering more than heavy praise.

passage: Gautam ran into the kitchen waving a sheet of paper. “Look! Look! It's Biscuit!” Biscuit is our cat. I'm Aadhya, his big sister, and I was cutting beans. Papa glanced up. “Wow, best artist in the whole world!” Gautam grinned for a second, then kept holding the paper up. Nani sat on the stool and looked for a long time. “Her whiskers go all the way out. And she's sleeping on the chappal, like always.” Gautam climbed onto her lap and showed her every stripe. I can't say what he was thinking, but he didn't go back to Papa.

qa.q: What is the cat in Gautam's drawing called?
qa.a: The cat is called Biscuit.

qa.q: What does Gautam still holding up the paper suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt proud but wanted more than a quick compliment, maybe hoping someone would really look; he may simply have been excited.

qa.q: What did Nani notice that Papa missed?
qa.a: Nani noticed the details, the whiskers and the cat sleeping on the chappal, showing she saw what Gautam actually drew.

qa.q: How does Aadhya read Gautam's choice to stay with Nani?
qa.a: Aadhya can't be sure of his thoughts but sees that he chose the person who shared the drawing with him, not the one with the biggest praise.

grounding: Shows a preschooler holding up a drawing and saying look, and shared delight in the details mattering more than heavy praise.

passage: Monday: Ira sat on the doorstep yanking at her laces until they knotted. Mohit, her big brother, showed her the bunny-ears loop twice. She kicked the shoe off. Wednesday: Ira practised on a shoe tied to the table leg, muttering, “Round the tree, into the hole.” Mohit did homework nearby. Saturday: “LOOK!” Ira hopped into the room on one foot, the other held up high. A floppy bow sat on top. Mohit dropped his pencil, crouched and tugged one loop. It held. They both whooped, and Ira untied it just to do it again while he watched.

qa.q: What did Ira practise on during Wednesday?
qa.a: Ira practised on a shoe tied to the table leg.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when she hopped in on one foot?
qa.a: She felt proud and thrilled at her floppy bow, eager for Mohit to see the result of days of effort 🎉

qa.q: Why did Mohit's reaction on Saturday work so well?
qa.a: He dropped what he was doing, checked the bow and cheered with her, which showed shared delight in her real effort rather than big words.

qa.q: What is it like for Mohit to watch Ira struggle on Monday?
qa.a: It may be frustrating when she kicks the shoe off, but by leaving her to practise he lets her own the success later.

grounding: Shows a young child holding up a tied shoe and shouting look after days of effort, met with shared delight rather than heavy praise.

passage: Parveen wandered from the sofa to the window to the fridge and back, dragging her feet across the Mumbai flat's tiles. “Uma Khala, what can I do-o-o?” Uma was typing a work email. “You can help me sort socks, or you can find something to do with this.” She tipped out a tin of clothes pegs. Parveen flopped on the floor and groaned. Five minutes later the groaning had stopped. Uma looked over. A row of pegs stood clipped along the sofa edge, each with a paper face. “It's a bus,” said Parveen. “That one's the driver. He's grumpy.”

qa.q: What did Uma tip out for Parveen?
qa.a: Uma tipped out a tin of clothes pegs.

qa.q: How was Parveen feeling as she wandered and asked what to do?
qa.a: She felt bored and restless, dragging her feet and whining; she may also have wanted Uma's attention while Uma worked.

qa.q: Why did offering two choices work here?
qa.a: The choices gave Parveen something to pick without Uma stopping work, and the plain tin of pegs left space for her own idea.

qa.q: What would change if Uma had handed Parveen a video on the phone instead?
qa.a: Parveen would probably stop whining, but she might not have invented the peg bus with its grumpy driver.

grounding: Shows a preschooler wandering and whining what can I do, an adult offering choices, and the boredom turning into a made-up game.

passage: “Dadi, I'm bored. The train is never coming.” “It's late, Rashmi. Maybe half an hour more.” “What can I do? There's nothing.” Rashmi hung off the bench arm, whining. Jyoti, her Dadi, looked round the platform. “Two choices. Count the red bags, or make up a story about that sleeping dog.” “Bags are boring.” “The dog, then.” Rashmi squinted at it. “He's… a train dog. He's waiting for his boss.” “Who's his boss?” “The driver! He's late 'cause he stopped for samosas.” Jyoti laughed. “And then?” Rashmi slid off the bench to sit nearer the dog, talking the whole time.

qa.q: How much longer did Jyoti think the train might take?
qa.a: Jyoti said maybe half an hour more.

qa.q: What does Rashmi hanging off the bench arm suggest about her mood?
qa.a: It suggests she felt bored and restless with nothing to do; she may also have been tired from the long wait.

qa.q: How did Jyoti's two choices help Rashmi?
qa.a: They let her pick something herself, and the story choice turned her boredom into a made-up tale.

qa.q: If you were Jyoti on that platform, what would you want Rashmi to discover?
qa.a: That even a dull wait can become fun when she uses her own imagination.

grounding: Shows a preschooler whining and asking what can I do during a long wait, and an adult offering choices that lead to a creative game.

passage: Camp note, day three. Ujjwal, play supervisor. During free play Karthik drifted between the swings, the sand and my chair six times in ten minutes. He whined, “What can I do? Everything is boring.” I didn't hand him a new game. I asked, “Do you want to be alone, with a friend, or with me?” He chose alone. I gave him two old cardboard tubes and left him. For a while he just lay on the mat. Then he started rolling pebbles through the tubes, and soon built a ramp with a chappal, timing the pebbles aloud.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal give Karthik?
qa.a: Ujjwal gave Karthik two old cardboard tubes.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling while he drifted and lay on the mat?
qa.a: He felt bored and restless, unsure what to do; lying still may also mean he was tired or simply waiting for an idea.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal ask Karthik to choose how he wanted to play?
qa.a: Letting him choose gave Karthik some control, and the free time with simple tubes left room for his own ramp idea.

qa.q: What would change if Ujjwal had filled every minute with games?
qa.a: Karthik might never feel bored, but he also might not have found the ramp idea on his own.

grounding: Shows a preschooler wandering and whining that everything is boring, an adult offering a choice, and boredom leading to a creative idea.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: Note, UKG class, Wednesday. Uma Ma'am. Gautam came in from the relay with bright red cheeks. When I called him up to put a star on the chart for helping, a boy shouted, “Gautam's blushing! Gautam's shy!” Gautam's face went even redder and he hid behind the cupboard door. I stopped the teasing: “In our class we don't laugh at people's faces.” Later, alone, I asked him, “Your cheeks were red. Were you hot from running, or did the star feel big?” He whispered, “Both.” I told him red cheeks come from lots of things, nothing to hide.

qa.q: Where did Gautam hide after the teasing?
qa.a: Gautam hid behind the cupboard door.

qa.q: What might have made Gautam's cheeks red?
qa.a: The relay may have made him hot, and being called up for a star may have made him feel shy or proud; he said both, so the redness had mixed causes.

qa.q: How did Uma handle the teasing and the question of why?
qa.a: She stopped the teasing at once and later asked privately with two gentle options, letting Gautam name his own reasons.

qa.q: How might the boy who shouted see things differently after Uma spoke?
qa.a: He might learn that red cheeks can come from running or from feelings, and that pointing them out made Gautam hide.

grounding: Shows a young child's red cheeks having several possible causes, teasing adding to shame, and a teacher gently naming the feelings instead.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: Sun beat down on the mango orchard. Harsha came back from the pump with a full bucket and cheeks as red as ripe fruit. A girl from the next farm waved at him. An uncle on the cot laughed. “Look, Harsha's gone red! Is it for your friend?” Harsha dropped the bucket and hid behind his Nana, Tanvir. Tanvir laid a wet towel on his head. “So many trips in this heat,” he told the uncle. Then, quietly, to Harsha: “Red from the sun, or from being looked at?” Harsha peeked out. “From the sun. And a little from him.”

qa.q: Where did Harsha hide?
qa.a: Harsha hid behind his Nana, Tanvir.

qa.q: Why did Harsha hide after the uncle laughed?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed at being teased about his red cheeks; his answer shows the heat mattered too, so both the sun and shame played a part.

qa.q: What small step did Tanvir take to calm things down?
qa.a: Tanvir cooled him with a wet towel, told the uncle about the heat and quietly asked Harsha which cause it was.

qa.q: How might the uncle see his joke after Tanvir's words?
qa.a: He might realise the red face could be from heat and work, and that his joke made the boy hide.

grounding: Shows a young child's red cheeks coming from heat and shyness at once, teasing increasing shame, and an adult gently helping him name it.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: After his solo at the end-of-year concert in Johannesburg, Mateo came off the stage with cheeks glowing pink. The hall was warm and he had sung loudly. An older boy in the wings grinned. “Tomato face!” Mateo's chin dropped. His teacher, Mrs Lindiwe Dube, knelt beside him. “Your cheeks are pink. Maybe it's the hot lights, maybe you're proud, maybe it felt a bit big up there. Any of those?” Mateo thought, then held up his thumb. “Proud. And hot.” “Both are good,” she said. Then she turned to the older boy. “We don't name people by their faces here.”

qa.q: What did the older boy call Mateo?
qa.a: The older boy called him “Tomato face”.

qa.q: What was Mateo feeling when his chin dropped?
qa.a: He likely felt embarrassed and a little hurt by the nickname, just after feeling proud of his solo.

qa.q: Why did Mrs Dube offer several possible reasons for the pink cheeks?
qa.a: Offering choices let Mateo name his own feeling instead of being told, and showed that pink cheeks don't have only one meaning.

qa.q: What would change if Mrs Dube had laughed along with the older boy?
qa.a: Mateo might feel ashamed of his cheeks and of singing, and could be less willing to go on stage again.

grounding: Shows a young child's pink cheeks with several possible causes, teasing adding to shame, and a teacher gently helping him name the feeling.
